parsed.justification: All standard policy sections are present (purpose, scope, roles, principles, requirements, exceptions, monitoring, references) and technical content is largely aligned with NIST SP 800-63B and ISO 27001:2022. Minor inconsistency: Section 5.4 mandates smart-card/PKI MFA for NR/NS/MISSION SECRET while the org context states 'no cross-domain identity federation' and PKI per domain — consistent — but Section 5.8 requires privileged passwords 'rotated after each use where possible' which slightly tensions with the no-forced-rotation stance in 5.3 (though justified for privileged accounts). Otherwise coherent and technically tight.
evidence_quotes: Routine periodic password changes (e.g., every 90 days) are NOT required unless mandated by higher authority
Must be generated randomly (minimum 20 characters), rotated after each use where possible, and protected by MFA at all times.
Mandatory for all NR, NS, and MISSION SECRET domains: Passwords must always be combined with smart-card or equivalent PKI token.

parsed.justification: The policy is clearly tailored to the NATO multinational detachment in Romania: it names the four classification domains (NU/NR/NS/MISSION SECRET), references the ISSM in J6 chain, NCIRC alignment, SOFA, host-nation law, framework-nation caveats, and the 40h/year training envelope. It stops short of a 5 because some sections (storage, lockout, hashing) remain generic and there is little reflection of COMSEC two-person integrity, TEMPEST/SCIF, or specific operational constraints unique to this detachment.
evidence_quotes: This policy applies to all NMD personnel (military, civilian, contractors), accounts, and information systems within the operational control of the detachment—covering all classification domains (NU, NR, NS, MISSION SECRET).
Mandatory for all NR, NS, and MISSION SECRET domains: Passwords must always be combined with smart-card or equivalent PKI token.
Where a framework nation or coalition partner imposes stricter controls, the higher standard will apply for affected systems and users.

parsed.justification: Citations are pervasive and largely accurate, mapping each control to specific NATO policies, NIST CSF subcategories, NIST SP 800-63B sections, ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A controls, and GDPR articles. However, some references are imprecise (e.g., NIST CSF 2.0 uses PR.AA rather than PR.AC subcategories — PR.AC is from CSF 1.1), and a few citations like 'NATO INFOSEC' are vague. No statements are flagged as unsupported, preventing a 5.
evidence_quotes: [NIST SP 800-63B §5.1.1.2, ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.5.15, NATO INFOSEC]
[GDPR Art. 5, Art. 32]

parsed.justification: The controls align with the organisation's resource envelope: 25-FTE security staff and theatre-level 24/7 SOC support continuous monitoring; PKI/smart-card MFA already exists per domain; 40-hour training requirement matches the stated profile. Compensating controls are explicitly offered for legacy systems, and exception handling respects the NATO accreditation chain and national caveats.
evidence_quotes: All users must complete annual cyber hygiene training, including secure password practices, as part of the NMD cybersecurity training requirement (minimum 40 hours/year).
Where technical constraints preclude compliance, compensating controls (e.g., increased monitoring, air-gapping) must be implemented and documented.
The Security Operations Centre (SOC) shall continuously monitor for password-related security events

parsed.justification: The policy systematically references the major applicable frameworks (NATO C-M(2002)49, AC/322-D(2017)0009, AJP-3.20, Cyber Defence Pledge, Romanian CSL/NIS2, GDPR, SOFA, NIST CSF 2.0, NIST SP 800-63B, ISO/IEC 27001:2022) and maps controls to specific clauses. However, NIS2-specific obligations (e.g. incident notification timelines) are not articulated, GDPR coverage is limited to a brief data-minimisation note without DPIA/breach-notification triggers, and potential conflicts (GDPR vs NATO classification handling, SOFA vs host-nation reach) are not explicitly acknowledged within this password-scoped policy.
evidence_quotes: Align with NATO, host-nation, and international frameworks (see references).
Where user passwords or reset data are considered personal data under GDPR, ensure compliance with data minimisation, storage limitation, and access control principles. [GDPR Art. 5, Art. 32]
Romanian Cybersecurity Law 58/2019 (NIS/NIS2)

parsed.justification: Nearly every substantive control in Section 5 carries an inline attribution to specific clauses (e.g., NIST SP 800-63B §5.1.1.2, ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.5.15/A.8.12/A.5.16, NATO AC/322-D(2017)0009, GDPR Art. 5/32, NIST CSF subcategories). Multiple frameworks are distinguished rather than lumped, and the references section closes the audit trail. Minor weaknesses (e.g., 'NATO INFOSEC' without a clause number in a couple of places) prevent perfection but do not materially undermine auditability.

parsed.justification: The policy makes only passing reference to the resource envelope, primarily through the training hours figure and an 'operational realism' principle. There is no explicit phasing, trade-off reasoning, or calibration of controls against the budget/staff envelope; controls are stated as absolutes with exceptions handled case-by-case rather than as resource-driven choices.
evidence_quotes: Operational Realism: Requirements reflect the detachment's operational tempo and multinational staffing.
All users must complete annual cyber hygiene training, including secure password practices, as part of the NMD cybersecurity training requirement (minimum 40 hours/year).
Where technical constraints preclude compliance, compensating controls (e.g., increased monitoring, air-gapping) must be implemented and documented.
